newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge urged to block Calif. measure.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge urged to block Calif. measure.

text.p: Civil rights lawyers urged a judge Monday to block temporarily a California ban on affirmative action, saying the measure would turn the "glass ceiling" for women and minorities into an "iron cage."

Civil rights groups, including the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), sued to block the anti-affirmative action measure a day after Californians voted 54-46 percent to approve it in the Nov. 5 election. They argue that the measure, Proposition 209, is unconstitutional.

Lawyers for the civil rights groups asked U.S. District Judge Thelton Henderson at a crowded hearing in San Francisco Monday to issue a temporary restraining order blocking Proposition 209 until a hearing is held on the merits of the case.

Henderson said he would consider the arguments and hoped to issue a ruling soon on the request for a restraining order. He said the issues were far-reaching and touched upon matters "of great significance to all Californians."
The suit names as defendants California Gov. Pete Wilson and state Attorney-General Dan Lungren, both Republicans and supporters of Proposition 209.

Proposition 209 bars discrimination or preferential treatment based on race or sex in public employment, education and contracting in California. Opponents say the initiative, the first of its kind, strikes a blow at 30 years of U.S. affirmative action policies aimed at broadening opportunities for women and racial minorities.
During the three-and-a-half hour hearing, ACLU attorney Edward Chen said Proposition 209 "turns the glass ceiling for women and minorities effectively into an iron cage."

Mark Rosenbaum, another ACLU attorney, said that under Proposition 209 women or members of racial minorities who had evidence of discrimination could not go to local government agencies and say "do something about it."
But California Deputy Attorney General Paul Dobson,arguing for the state, said Proposition 209 banned discrimination and gave equal protection to everyone regardless of race or gender.

Civil rights groups maintain that Proposition 209 violates the equal protection clause of the U.S. constitution because they say it would block legislation needed to protect minorities and women from discrimination.

They argue it violates the supremacy clause of the constitution -- which forbids states from obstructing federal law -- by outlawing state and local programmes established to ensure compliance with federal civil rights laws.
